body: I am by no means an expert in the rendering space or C++ so any feedback on making this PR cleaner and more memory safe is much appreciated.  I saw a problem that I figured could be solved with some data structure refactoring and simply went at it for a couple days.

> The new code should be compatible with the old shader syntax, allowing new methods to be used as advanced options to replace the rendering mode defined by the shader. This change is too disruptive and definitely cannot be merged; it would cause all existing plugins with shaders to throw errors, which is terrible. It seems like it could be implemented using shader instances, where instances can override the scene rendering mode of the template, requiring less modification to the engine.

Everything within this refactor keeps existing functionality exactly as-is, and simply unlocks the users ability to add more than what Godot provides out of the box.  There is nothing in this code that disrupts how existing shaders work, and specifically the intent of this PR over the alternatives referenced is to avoid introducing new syntax to shaders.  There should be absolutely no case where existing plugins would break, as there are no API breaking changes, and the rendering functionality should yield identical behavior for existing projects.

The majority of this PR's changes are a refactoring that just replaces switch statements to referencing structs to guide behavior.  This is done because it's more practical to define rendering strategies as a singular pattern than to add a completely conditional flow on top of the existing logic just to support user defined blend modes.

> This feature is not very practical. The only scenario requiring switching scene rendering modes is when particle effects are involved. Most particle effect shaders have very few variations, so writing the code multiple times has little impact. Therefore, the current practical method used in the Godot engine is fine.

There are many use cases where the existing blend modes are *not* sufficient, as referenced in this PR and proposals.  I have personally hit a wall with supporting Live2D in Godot because of this limitation.

I think I may have caused confusion with using incorrect terminology pertaining to shaders with the PRs title and initial code.

This PR is looking to expand only *blending* capabilities.  This does not introduce new shader types, nor does it allow users to define new render_mode keywords.  It only allows for new *options* for blending, so instead of just `blend_mix`, `blend_add`, etc., you can now add your own (such as `blend_direct` in the example) in case the visuals you are attempting to render require different blend factors.

The approach taken in this PR is proposed because other PRs attempting to expose factors directly in the shaders with new keywords were considered exposing too many details to the users and shader language surface area.  Exposing blend factors is a use case that exists and needed by developers, we just need to agree upon how to do it, because I feel the current solution of forcing people to use RenderingDevice is overkill.  As there were already structs available for describing the desired functionality, I tried to expand upon how they're used.

Specific blend functions are handled by the rendering drivers, not materials, so you can not simply extend materials to use different blend functions.  The "blend mode" that exists is just metadata, to a preconfigured, hard-coded set of blend factors.  Within Godot, it is not currently possible the achieve what you are suggesting without making changes to expose that ability, hence why there are proposals and have been lengthy discussion on the subject to devise a user-friendly approach.

Currently the only way to work around Godot's offered blend modes is to go through the RenderingDevice interface, which is not available on all platforms and makes non-trivial work out of a trivial setting that many graphics artists depend on having control over.  I am interested in adding blend modes without having to propose new ones to be baked into the engine for every permutation an artist can come up with.

It helps to expose it in shaders as they are the middle ground between high-level materials and low-level rendering APIs.  This PR improves shader capability and usability for artists, while importantly NOT breaking existing shader behavior and exposing the functionality for ALL rendering targets.

Here's an example of blending for Live2D models being fixed with this change. [Before:](https://github.com/erodozer/open-vt/issues/23#issuecomment-3900389173) With PR: By allowing for custom blend modes, I'm able to [replicate the functions](https://github.com/MizunagiKB/gd_cubism/issues/7#issuecomment-3902411403) used by Live2D's reference implementation so that Godot can match the rendering behavior in other engines, such as Unity.
